name: Yusuf Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Yusuf, and thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, how would you describe your work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm foreman at Brandt's, a family farm east of town with about 600 pigs, some beef stores, and maize and wheat for feed. Old Mr Brandt and his wife own it, their son does the selling, and I run the day to day with two other lads. Nineteen years now. It pays well for farm work, and between that, Lena's job and the little flat my dad left me, we're comfortable.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Six o'clock I walk the pig sheds, check the water lines, the feeders, any sow that's about to farrow. Then it's mucking out, moving weaners, and in the season I'm on the drill or the forage harvester. I like a job done right and a shed that smells as it should. What wears me out is things changing for the sake of it; they put in a new feed computer three years ago and I still do the rounds by hand to check it, because I don't trust it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nothing much, to be honest. Maybe that the people who sold all this got rich and we got another screen. I don't go online to talk about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep doing what I do. Good. I've got a job I'm good at, a house half paid for and money behind me. I don't need the world to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Same hours, same sheds, same savings going in at the end of the month. Maybe I'd let the son put another sensor in if he must, and I'd keep checking it by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Calm. It's the kind of news you hear on the radio and forget by dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Lena uses something on her phone for recipes. I've got the same phone I had six years ago and I use it for calls and the weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd want from this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For people to stop talking about it, honestly. Every farm meeting it's drones and data. I'd like one meeting about the price of pig feed.

S0.say: I'd say nothing much, maybe that the people who sold all this got rich and we got another screen. I don't talk about it online.
S0.think: It means I keep doing what I do, and that's good. I've got a job I'm good at, a half-paid house and money behind me.
S0.do: Carries on with the same hours, sheds and monthly savings. Lets the farm's son add sensors if he insists, and keeps checking them by hand.
S0.feel: Calm, the kind of news you forget by dinner.
S0.quote: I'd like one meeting about the price of pig feed.
S0.fieldNote: Yusuf is quietly content and wants nothing to change. He does not use AI at all and checks the existing feed computer by hand. He blames no one, but he is tired of the talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's how business goes. Some change helps, some doesn't. I'd keep my head down at work and let the son and his gadgets argue it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd lose some of what I like. The son's been on about robot cleaners for the sheds, and a camera system that weighs pigs as they walk past. I'd still be needed, but I'd be watching screens, and I'm no good at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year and see what they actually put in. I'd put a bit more aside, maybe an extra hundred and fifty a month. If they made me learn a computer system, I'd learn the least I could and keep checking by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep, but I'd notice it on the drive in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the Brandts brought in more machines, what would your part look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably still foreman on paper, but half my rounds would be on a tablet. I'd hate that. I'd still walk the sheds, though, they can't stop me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: There are other farms nearby. Would you move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could, there's plenty of farms around. But I've been there nineteen years. Mr Brandt came to my dad's funeral. You don't just move for a few machines.

S1.say: I'd say it's how business goes, some change helps and some doesn't. I'd keep my head down and let the son and his gadgets argue it out.
S1.think: I think I'd lose some of what I like, with robot cleaners and cameras weighing the pigs. I'd still be needed, but I'd be watching screens, and I'm no good at that.
S1.do: Waits a year to see what's installed and puts about 150 more a month into savings. Learns only the minimum of any new system and keeps checking by hand.
S1.feel: A mild unease he notices on the drive to work.
S1.quote: I'd still walk the sheds, though, they can't stop me.
S1.fieldNote: Yusuf's resistance is gentle but firm. He would stay out of loyalty to the farm family rather than look elsewhere, even with jobs nearby. He frames change as just business, with no villain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a mess and nobody planned it. I wouldn't blame the Brandts, they'd be forced to keep up. I might blame government a bit for being asleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm done. A robot that can farrow sows and run a harvester doesn't need me. I've never used one of these AI things and two years isn't enough for me to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cut back first: no holiday, no new car, the kids' extras trimmed. Keep the rent from the flat coming in, that's our steady money. I'd lean on Lena's brother, he's got a building firm, if he still has one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the ground going soft under your feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. What does that short warning change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, there's no time to do it my way, which is slowly. I'd just be standing there while it happens. That's what scares me, more than the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, we've got the flat and we've got savings, so we're not on the street. Then probably nothing more, I'm not a talker. She'd know anyway.

S2.say: I'd say it's a mess nobody planned. I wouldn't blame the Brandts for keeping up, but I might blame government for being asleep.
S2.think: I think I'm done. A robot that can farrow sows and run a harvester doesn't need me, and two years is too short for me to start with AI.
S2.do: Cuts the holiday, a new car and the children's extras. Relies on rent from his flat as steady income and leans on his brother-in-law's building firm for possible work.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like the ground going soft underfoot, more about losing control than about money.
S2.quote: There's no time to do it my way, which is slowly.
S2.fieldNote: Yusuf's savings and rental flat keep him from panic, but the speed takes away his slow way of handling change. He blames government lightly and the farm family not at all. He'd tell his partner the practical facts and little else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Much the same. It's coming, best get ready, no point shouting. I'd say that over a pint and leave it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd still lose the job, but I'd see it coming. Five years is long enough to put a good bit more by. I still don't see myself learning robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, maybe five hundred a month, and pay the mortgage down. Watch what the Brandts do and how the other farms go. If I saw a job that was still safe and still outdoors, I'd look at it, but only in the last year or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less than the fast one, but there's a clock ticking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years instead of two, would you do anything differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd let them choose, but I'd say don't pick something a machine does. Hana likes drawing, Kai likes football. Neither of them wants to farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Hana and Kai?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: And the flat. I'd do it up properly so it keeps renting. That's the one thing that pays without me lifting a fork.

S3.say: I'd say it's coming, so best get ready and there's no point shouting. I'd say that over a pint and leave it there.
S3.think: I think I'd still lose the job, but I'd see it coming and could put more by. I still don't see myself learning robots.
S3.do: Saves around 500 a month and pays down the mortgage while watching how nearby farms change. Refurbishes the rental flat and only looks at other outdoor jobs in the last year or two.
S3.feel: Anxious, with a clock ticking, though less than in the fast picture.
S3.quote: That's the one thing that pays without me lifting a fork.
S3.fieldNote: Extra time makes Yusuf save harder rather than change. He relies on the rental flat as his real safety net. His advice to his children is cautious and practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so let's be sensible about it. No panic. I'm not one for big speeches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 by then, mortgage gone, kids nearly done with school. I'd probably be fine. Not happy, but fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year, nothing new. I'd keep saving and keep working. Maybe in five or six years I'd do a heavy goods driving licence or a machinery ticket as a backup, something with an engine I understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a long way off. Like hearing thunder over the next county.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Is there anything you'd start this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, no. I'd keep going and see. I don't like jumping at things that haven't happened, I never have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd wait. Is there a point where you'd stop waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the Brandts sit me down. That'll be the day. Until then I've got pigs to feed.

S4.say: I'd say there's time, so let's be sensible and not panic. I'm not one for big speeches about it.
S4.think: I'd be 53 by then, mortgage gone and kids nearly done with school. I'd probably be fine, not happy but fine.
S4.do: Starts nothing new this year and keeps saving and working. Considers a heavy goods driving licence or machinery ticket in five or six years as a backup.
S4.quote: When the Brandts sit me down. That'll be the day. Until then I've got pigs to feed.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Yusuf go back to what he likes best: waiting. He'd only move when his employer tells him, and his backup idea is a familiar kind of machine. His pragmatism is about patience, not planning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I can handle things if they come slowly, but that one doesn't give me time. What would help is some way to keep working with my hands, even if it's paid less, and the government having some kind of plan ready instead of making it up.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about loyalty. I've stayed at one farm nineteen years because that's how I was raised. If machines come, I'd like the farms to stay loyal back, even a little.

headlineQuote: I can handle things if they come slowly, but that one doesn't give me time.
portrait: Yusuf Nakamura is a 43-year-old foreman at Brandt's, a family pig, beef and feed crop farm, where he's worked nineteen years. He's comfortable, with a good wage, a partner who works, savings and a rental flat his father left him, and he wants nothing to change. He never uses AI and checks the existing feed computer by hand. He stays calm or uneasy in the slower pictures but is alarmed by AGI in two years because it takes away his slow way of coping. He blames nobody much, and values loyalty between workers and farms.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it wouldn't give him time to handle change slowly.
whatWouldHelp: A way to keep working with his hands even for less pay, and a government plan ready in advance.
